{"id": "89:29/q11", "question": "What events are reported in connection with this address?", "turns_on": "Different reports name Ḥamza, Khubayb or ʿUthmān as an occasion; other narrations concern Ibn ʿAbbās's funeral or the believer's grave, while al-Rāzī applies the wording generally.", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q11/p1", "position": "It was revealed concerning Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this occasion without establishing it; Abū Ḥayyān also lists Ḥamza. Al-Rāzī insists the wording remains general regardless of a specific occasion."}, {"id": "89:29/q11/p2", "position": "It was revealed concerning Khubayb ibn ʿAdī when he was crucified by Meccans.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says God answered Khubayb's prayer that his face turn toward the sacred city and no one could turn it away; one version says he faced Medina. Abū Ḥayyān also lists Khubayb. Al-Rāzī retains the wording's general force."}, {"id": "89:29/q11/p3", "position": "It was revealed concerning ʿUthmān after he bought the well of Rūma for public drinking.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits a report from Ibn ʿAbbās about God's invitation to buy the well and the subsequent revelation; Abū Ḥayyān also lists ʿUthmān."}, {"id": "89:29/q11/p4", "position": "At Ibn ʿAbbās's burial in Ṭāʾif, an unusual bird entered his bier and did not emerge, and an unseen speaker recited these verses at his grave.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's report appears in Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī and al-Durr; descriptions vary between bier and coffin and between recitation at the grave and after burial."}, {"id": "89:29/q11/p5", "position": "A believer rests in a spacious, illuminated grave, while an unbeliever is directed to torment.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr: Quranic or sunlike light illumines the believer's grave and the believer sleeps like a bride until awakened by a beloved; the unbeliever receives a foul coarse covering."}, {"id": "89:29/q11/p6", "position": "Specific reports do not restrict the address to their named persons.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the general wording governs beyond a particular cause, despite the Ḥamza and Khubayb reports."}]}
{"id": "89:29/q12", "question": "What reward is reported for reciting this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q12/p1", "position": "Recitation during the ten nights brings forgiveness; recitation at other times brings light on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Bayḍāwī report the same Prophetic promise without grading it in these notes."}]}
{"id": "89:29/q13", "question": "How does this verse close the sūra and relate to its other verses?", "turns_on": "How the final promise relates to earlier warning and testing, and whether the closing verses are a later addition or part of the original sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q13/p1", "position": "It adds glad tidings for the faithful after warning and punishment, encouraging good and deterring evil.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Quran joins promise to warning; he links this address to the preceding crushing of the earth and treats intervening material as parenthetical if the sequence is one revelation. Corpus Coranicum says the final positive afterlife ending answers the Hell scene in 89:23 and God's speech supersedes human responses to worldly allotment and threatened Hell. It calls verses 27–30 a later addition, whereas Ibn ʿĀshūr infers one original sequence from recitation and codex order. Iṣlāḥī sees the peaceful soul as passing the sura's tests of wealth, deprivation, gratitude, patience and others' rights."}, {"id": "89:29/q13/p2", "position": "The peaceful life among the righteous resembles the ten nights, and Garden entry the festival dawn.", "reasons": "Elmalılı proposes this correspondence with the opening oath and Eid al-Adha imagery."}]}
{"id": "89:29/q14", "question": "Should the two entry commands form one verse or be divided?", "turns_on": "Whether semantic continuity outweighs an approximate end rhyme in assigning the verse boundary.", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q14/p1", "position": "The two imperatives belong together, so the Kufan division between them is unsuitable.", "reasons": "Neuwirth argues their close relation requires keeping them together."}, {"id": "89:29/q14/p2", "position": "The division is supported by an approximate rhyme between ʿibādī and jannatī.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum counters Neuwirth by allowing nonclassical vowel and consonant variation, as in other Quranic pairs in 89:15–16, 23–24 and 27–28."}]}
{"id": "89:29/q15", "question": "What inward or spiritual lesson is drawn from entering among God's servants?", "turns_on": "Whether the command describes realized spiritual communion or can be applied as an ongoing earthly practice; al-Ālūsī rejects the latter as tafsīr.", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q15/p1", "position": "It signifies realized servitude and communion with God's special servants.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the special servants realize essential unity. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the soul relinquishes independence and submits its being, actions and choices to God. Al-Rāzī likens purified souls to mirrors increasing one another's radiance and spiritual rank, citing 56:90–91; al-Ālūsī calls the mirror account rhetorical speculation."}, {"id": "89:29/q15/p2", "position": "Throughout life, turn to God, join sincere servants by good works, and potentially enter the Garden.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this inward application but says it is not a sound interpretation. Elmalılı separately urges worldly righteous effort through the causative fā."}]}
{"id": "89:29/q16", "question": "What other textual echoes or devotional uses accompany this phrase?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q16/p1", "position": "The request to be admitted among righteous servants echoes Solomon's prayer.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Baghawī cite 27:19; Study Quran joins it with 29:9."}, {"id": "89:29/q16/p2", "position": "The word ʿabd is cross-referenced to 53:10.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum supplies the cross-reference without an additional explanation."}, {"id": "89:29/q16/p3", "position": "The promise can be voiced as a prayer for the commentator and readers to return content, join sincere servants, and attain Paradise and God's vision.", "reasons": "Elmalılı closes his discussion with this supplication."}]}
{"id": "89:29/q17", "question": "When is the believer promised Paradise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q17/p1", "position": "At death, gathering, and resurrection.", "reasons": "A report from Abū Usāma ibn Zayd from his father and Zayd ibn Aslam gives these three moments of good news, without choosing just one moment for the entry command."}]}
{"id": "89:29/q18", "question": "What is Paradise for the servants admitted to it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:29/q18/p1", "position": "It is the eternal home and dwelling of the righteous and virtuous.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī attributes this description to the majority."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q01", "question": "How is the command to enter read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted plural, singular, explicit body, and expanded codex wordings, and whether singular servant denotes one body or the servants collectively.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q01/p1", "position": "The common reading has the plural 'My servants' followed by 'enter My Garden'.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ contrasts the common plural with Ibn ʿAbbās's singular; al-Zajjāj prefers the majority reading and interpretation; Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh transmits the ordinary wording."}, {"id": "89:30/q01/p2", "position": "A variant has singular 'My servant'.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ attributes it to Ibn ʿAbbās alone, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ālūsī list Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Yamānī, Mujāhid, Abū Jaʿfar and others. Al-Kalbī and Abū Shaykh understand the spirit entering a body; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also allows singular ʿabd to be generic, as believers are one hand. Corpus Coranicum refers ʿabd to 53:10."}, {"id": "89:30/q01/p3", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd's reading explicitly says to enter the body of God's servant.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī invokes this reading to support taking the addressed soul as a spirit entering bodies."}, {"id": "89:30/q01/p4", "position": "Ubayy's codex expands the address and concludes with entry into God's servant.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports wording that first has the soul return to its Lord content and pleasing; Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the expanded address to the assured soul."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q02", "question": "Why does entry among servants take fī while entry into the Garden takes a direct object?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q02/p1", "position": "Fī marks entry into a nonliteral sphere, while a real container is entered directly.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān contrasts figurative containment in the servants with literal Garden containment. Al-Ālūsī repeats his explanation. Al-Burhān distinguishes physical and conceptual container and contents, taking physical containment as literal and one mixed metaphor as closest to it."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q03", "question": "When is entry into the Garden commanded or promised?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is at death, in the grave interval, at resurrection, after judgment, or at several stages; and whether Garden entry is immediate or final.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q03/p1", "position": "The entry commands are spoken at resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk place the soul's return to its body then; al-Ṭabarī prefers this because the next words command entry among servants and Garden. Abū Ṣāliḥ distinguishes departure at death from entry commands on Resurrection. ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk put the address there; al-Qaffāl treats the imperative as a future report in meaning."}, {"id": "89:30/q03/p2", "position": "The address comes after resurrection and completed reckoning.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites the context, including 89:24, an

d finds this the most apparent timing, while allowing other reports to fit. Al-Ālūsī reports an after-reckoning reading of return to the promised Garden and righteous company; the claimed prior residence is explained by potential presence in Adam's loins."}, {"id": "89:30/q03/p3", "position": "The soul is addressed at death and enters the company of the near servants then, while the lasting Garden follows at resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and a group place the address at death; al-Ālūsī distinguishes immediate spiritual company from deferred lasting bodily Paradise and says certainty permits future fulfillment to be expressed as immediate. Al-Ḥasan describes God taking a believer's soul, mutual satisfaction, and admitting it among the righteous into Paradise."}, {"id": "89:30/q03/p4", "position": "Both entries can occur immediately after death, with provisional enjoyment of Paradise before the Hour.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports joining righteous souls or their bodies and temporary Garden enjoyment; he cites a hadith placing believers' souls in birds' crops in Paradise and an athar granting a believer half the promised Garden at death."}, {"id": "89:30/q03/p5", "position": "The believer is given the good news of Paradise at death, resurrection, and gathering.", "reasons": "Usāma ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Aslam transmit three stages; al-Māwardī's version names death, resurrection and Paradise itself. Ibn Kathīr says angels announce it at death and rising from the grave. Elmalılı allows each death to count as a person's resurrection or the commands to be treated together."}, {"id": "89:30/q03/p6", "position": "The address comes after death but before resurrection, when the soul is shown its future Garden home and returned for grave questioning.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī says the believer sees the Garden home, returns to the body, and awaits Munkar and Nakīr; al-Ālūsī gives no grading of the report."}, {"id": "89:30/q03/p7", "position": "The commands can address the soul continually in earthly life.", "reasons": "An inward application calls for turning to God in every matter, joining sincere servants by good works, and potential Garden entry. Al-Ālūsī explicitly says this does not count as a sound interpretation."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q04", "question": "What does God's Garden here designate?", "turns_on": "Whether the possessive names the ordinary promised abode, mercy, a highest particular garden, or a further divine life.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q04/p1", "position": "Paradise, the lasting abode and prepared reward of the righteous.", "reasons": "The majority in al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī identify the eternal dwelling. Al-Ṭabrisī says it is promised and prepared with delights; al-Bayḍāwī calls it the abode of reward; al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī stress bodily happiness. Al-Kāshshāf, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Elmalılı say entry is together with God's servants. The Study Quran says most take the Garden as Paradise generally."}, {"id": "89:30/q04/p2", "position": "God's Garden means His mercy or protective care.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Garden entry is through the mercy entered among God's servants; Muḥammad ibn Muzāḥim and al-Ḍaḥḥāk gloss it as mercy. Sayyid Quṭb adds protection and secure closeness rooted in trust in God's decree."}, {"id": "89:30/q04/p3", "position": "It is the Garden of Eden, highest of the gardens.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī identifies this particular Garden with the highest garden."}, {"id": "89:30/q04/p4", "position": "It is the Garden of God's Essence or Presence.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls it the garden particular to God, of the Essence; the Study Quran reports a highest Garden of the Divine Essence in God's Presence among progressive hereafter levels."}, {"id": "89:30/q04/p5", "position": "Two paradises are involved: the Garden itself and life and permanence through divine life and permanence.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī distinguishes the Garden from this further divine mode of life and permanence."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q05", "question": "What reward is expressed by the two entries, and why is the Garden mentioned second?", "turns_on": "How the company of servants relates to Paradise: a distinct superior spiritual reward followed by bodily reward, or the linked fulfillment of the faithful soul's life.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q05/p1", "position": "Joining the servants is the superior spiritual happiness; Garden entry completes it with bodily happiness.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts immediate spiritual felicity with bodily Paradise after the great Resurrection, accounting for fa versus wa; al-Ālūsī says superior spiritual companionship is ordered first. Al-Thaʿlabī reports an inverted sequence explaining entry into Paradise with God's servants."}, {"id": "89:30/q05/p2", "position": "Entry among the servants and into Paradise marks the contented soul's successful final outcome.", "reasons": "Elmalılı describes the soul's life among the righteous as ten nights before Eid al-Adha and Paradise as the dawn of the greatest feast; Islahi says the soul passed the test of fortune and hardship, fulfilling others' rights, gratitude and patience. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says abandoning independence and submitting being, acts and choices establish complete servitude. Kuranyolu cites 9:72 for divine pleasure as a greater final gift; Elmalılı prays for this company, Paradise and vision of God."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q06", "question": "Why is the Garden called 'My Garden'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q06/p1", "position": "The first-person possessive honors the Garden and its recipient.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the honor to the seat of truth with the Mighty King in 54:55; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this special possessive occurs nowhere else in the Qurʾān. Kuranyolu similarly treats 'My servants' as supreme honor."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q07", "question": "What explains the shift to God's first-person speech?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q07/p1", "position": "'My servants' and 'My Garden' shift from the preceding third-person mention of 'your Lord', and the Garden's possessive makes the shift fitting.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes this change of person in both possessives and finds the attribution of Paradise to God especially apt after the third-person reference."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q08", "question": "Why is 'enter' repeated before the Garden?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q08/p1", "position": "Repeating the command emphasizes Garden entry and heightens the recipients' joy.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says a single verb could have governed both objects; spelling out the two entries details the previous general good news and renews joy."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q09", "question": "How should the divine commands be understood as speech?", "turns_on": "Whether an omitted future speech formula governs the imperatives or the sūra closes with a direct present address.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q09/p1", "position": "An implied 'God will say' makes the address a future declaration and creative command.", "reasons": "Elmalılı attributes this to the majority and connects it to the preceding context; al-Qaffāl likewise says the imperative has report meaning."}, {"id": "89:30/q09/p2", "position": "They can be a direct legislative address heard by tranquil souls now.", "reasons": "Elmalılı finds the separated closing address plausible, with direct hearing of the promise; Kuranyolu says the unintroduced address is a warm honor bringing afterlife happiness into present life."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q10", "question": "How does entry among God's servants relate to this Garden entry?", "turns_on": "Whether the servants are righteous companions, obedience, bodies receiving spirits, or proximate spirits; the mirror explanation is expressly disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q10/p1", "position": "The soul joins the righteous or chosen servants and enters Paradise with them.", "reasons": "Qatāda repeatedly glosses the servants as the righteous; Abū ʿUbayda says 'with' or 'among' the chosen and cites 27:19. Ibn ʿAṭiyya places them at the gathering when Hell-bound people separate. Al-Kāshshāf, al-Qurṭubī and others take the two commands as entry with God's servants."}, {"id": "89:30/q10/p2", "position": "Entering the servants means entering God's obedience, and Garden entry means entering His mercy.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Muḥammad ibn Muzāḥim interpret the two commands through obedience and mercy, making the second depend on the first."}, {"id": "89:30/q10/p3", "position": "The spirit enters bodies, then the prepared reward.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī reads the singular servant as the spirit's return to a body; Abū Shaykh says likewise. Ibn Masʿūd's reading explicitly supplies body. Al-Ālūsī cites Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr construing the plural generically as bodies; another analysis makes 'Lord' the soul's bodily owner."}, {"id": "89:30/q10/p4", "position": "The soul joins the proximate spirits, whose lights reflect upon one another.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and Elmalılı report mutual radiance like facing mirrors. Al-Ālūsī rejects the polished-mirror image, its increasing knowledge, as rhetorical speculation; this does not reject proximity itself."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q11", "question": "What does the preceding 'return to your Lord' mean in relation to these entries?", "turns_on": "The time of the address and whether 'Lord' denotes God, His promise or command, or the body's owner; 'return' also raises the issue of prior residence.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q11/p1", "position": "It is departure from worldly life at death, before the resurrection entry commands.", "reasons": "Abū Ṣāliḥ distinguishes the death-time return from the commands at resurrection; al-Ḥasan describes the believer's soul resting in God at death."}, {"id": "89:30/q11/p2", "position": "It is return to the promised destination of Paradise and righteous company after judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports t

he reply to the objection that 'return' presupposes previous residence: souls were potentially in Adam's loins in the Garden. He compares reports from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās reading maʿād in 28:85 as Paradise, while noting dependence on the disputed claim that Adam's Garden is the final Garden."}, {"id": "89:30/q11/p3", "position": "It is return to God's gracious command, treatment or honored station.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explains the return as being treated without distress and placed in a station of honor."}, {"id": "89:30/q11/p4", "position": "It is return to God's general favor from the intermediate realm or from the period around resurrection and judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives alternative starting points in barzakh, after resurrection or after judgment."}, {"id": "89:30/q11/p5", "position": "The person returns to God's station at resurrection.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk take nafs as the person, rabb as God and supply an omitted station."}, {"id": "89:30/q11/p6", "position": "The spirit returns to its body's owner before joining the servants and reward.", "reasons": "This construes rabb as the body formerly owned by the soul and makes the Garden the later abode of reward."}, {"id": "89:30/q11/p7", "position": "At death the soul returns to God's sacred realm and joins His near servants.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and a group place the address at death; al-Ālūsī makes nafs the spirit and the return to the holy realm."}, {"id": "89:30/q11/p8", "position": "The soul returns to its body for questioning after seeing its Garden home at death.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb specifies the interval before resurrection and Munkar and Nakīr."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q12", "question": "To whom does this promise apply?", "turns_on": "Whether named occasions restrict the addressee; al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī argue the wording reaches all believers.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q12/p1", "position": "It applies generally to faithful, tranquil souls; named persons are illustrative occasions.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and al-Farrāʾ give the general reading; al-Kashshāf calls it apparent. Al-Nasafī says the lesson follows general wording, and al-Ālūsī says named Companions are examples within that wording. Qatāda identifies the assured believer; Elmalılı and Islahi describe the contented soul that succeeds in the test."}, {"id": "89:30/q12/p2", "position": "Abū Bakr is promised this address.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports the verse was recited while Abū Bakr sat with the Prophet and admired it; the Prophet said an angel would say it to him at death. Al-Ālūsī cites a similar al-Ḥākim al-Tirmidhī version."}, {"id": "89:30/q12/p3", "position": "It was revealed about ʿUthmān after he purchased the Rūma well for public drinking.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and a report through Ibn ʿAbbās associate revelation with the endowment; al-Ālūsī names the route through Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and regards this as an example, not a limit."}, {"id": "89:30/q12/p4", "position": "It was revealed about Ḥamza.", "reasons": "Burayda transmits this identification; al-Ālūsī treats it as an illustrative case."}, {"id": "89:30/q12/p5", "position": "It concerns Khubayb ibn ʿAdī.", "reasons": "Reports say God turned his face toward the qibla after his captors turned it toward Medina, and they could not turn it back; al-Ālūsī treats him as an example."}, {"id": "89:30/q12/p6", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the soul as the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites a report through Ibn Mardawayh and treats this too as illustrative."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q13", "question": "What report connects this verse with Ibn ʿAbbās's burial?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q13/p1", "position": "A strange bird entered Ibn ʿAbbās's bier at Ṭāʾif and was not seen leaving; an unseen voice recited the tranquil-soul verses at his grave.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr transmits the event in several sources; versions say coffin or bier and place the recitation at the grave or its edge."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q14", "question": "What other death reports are connected with the verse?", "turns_on": "Different reports describe different persons and events rather than competing details of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q14/p1", "position": "A captive martyr's severed head recited the verse in Roman lands, leading three apostates back to Islam.", "reasons": "Qubāth ibn Razīn Abū Hāshim recounts the event in Ibn Kathīr."}, {"id": "89:30/q14/p2", "position": "At death the believer rests in a spacious, illuminated grave like a sleeping bride, while the unbeliever is sent to torment.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr reports light from the Qurʾān or like the sun and a foul coarse covering for the unbeliever."}, {"id": "89:30/q14/p3", "position": "Angels direct the solitary to Paradise homes, but they seek a good life solely with God.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī reports the solitary say they withdrew for God alone and sought no other object."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q15", "question": "What reward is reported for reciting Sūrat al-Fajr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q15/p1", "position": "Recitation during the ten nights brings forgiveness; recitation on other days brings light on Resurrection Day.", "reasons": "The report is ascribed to the Prophet in al-Kashshāf and the two al-Bayḍāwī notes."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q16", "question": "What does the passage imply about the soul's existence before embodiment?", "turns_on": "Whether 'return' entails a soul's existence before its body.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q16/p1", "position": "Some readings suggest souls existed before bodies in a realm of dominion or the unseen.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī presents this as a possible implication of the return language."}, {"id": "89:30/q16/p2", "position": "Most theologians and Plato's followers hold that souls are created when bodies become ready.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records this counterview without deciding it here."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q17", "question": "What inward account of the soul's path is given?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward meaning is a journey from worldly attachment, a scheme of soul stations, or an attempted literal timing in earthly life that al-Ālūsī rejects.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q17/p1", "position": "The soul attached to worldly life must leave it and follow the path of the afterlife toward God.", "reasons": "Ahl al-ishāra in al-Baghawī interpret return to God as abandoning worldly attachment."}, {"id": "89:30/q17/p2", "position": "The tranquil, content and approved soul are three spiritual stations.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this three-rank account to Sufi teachers, referring the details to their books."}, {"id": "89:30/q17/p3", "position": "The earthly-life commands describe continual obedience, sincere company and potential Garden entry.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the reading but says it is not sound exegesis."}]}
{"id": "89:30/q18", "question": "How does this ending relate to the rest of Sūrat al-Fajr?", "turns_on": "Whether the close is read as the sūra's integrated promise and oath fulfillment or as a later positive expansion of its earlier threat.", "positions": [{"id": "89:30/q18/p1", "position": "It completes warning with good news to believing souls, encouraging good and deterring evil.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr sees the usual joining of promise and warning; Sayyid Quṭb hears secure closeness after the earlier scenes, and Islahi ties the peaceful soul to success in the trial of wealth, deprivation and duties to others."}, {"id": "89:30/q18/p2", "position": "The ending fulfills the dawn oath through resurrection and the soul's festival-like arrival in Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says resurrection is the apparent subject of the opening oath at 89:1, without which creation would be vain; he praises the composition's inimitability.
